The blades are among the most expensive components of a wind turbine, accounting for 10-20% of total manufacturing costs.
Larger and more flexible blades have lower safety margins and are more susceptible to damage mechanisms like cracks and delaminations.
Damage in wind turbine blades can lead to critical failures that can damage not only the turbine they are attached to, but also nearby turbines.
The SCADA data used in this work has a low-pass filter applied, with 10-minute averages of the signals.
The edge frequencies of the blades were used as the primary structural health indicator, as they are sensitive to changes in blade stiffness.
The three blades on a turbine were found to have linear correlations in their edge frequencies during normal healthy conditions.
Out of the environmental and operational variables considered, only the ambient temperature had a systematic influence on the blade edge frequencies.
The training data for the GPs was selected from the first 2 years of turbine operation, with 2500 randomly selected data points.
The Gaussian Process hyperparameters were learned by maximizing the log marginal likelihood using the Nelder-Mead optimization algorithm.
X-bar control charts were used to monitor the averages of the GP residuals, with 3-sigma thresholds calculated over an initial 6-month period.
The proposed SHM system successfully identified early onset of damage in the case studies, up to 6 months before it was identified and remedied.
Computational costs of training the GPs scale cubically with the number of training points, so a balance had to be struck between accuracy and efficiency.
The versatility of the proposed methodology means it can also be applied to offshore wind turbines.
The use of SCADA data instead of higher-resolution data saves considerable processing time.
The normalization of data was done to avoid numerical instabilities and to not disclose confidential blade property information.
